More US lawmakers seek new AI rules after Anthropic researchers warn of human extinction. Growing numbers of US lawmakers are calling for new rules to govern artificial intelligence (AI) systems after dire warnings from two Anthropic researchers that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future. Alarm about the potential harm from AI grew this week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said he had resigned , and that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger chimed in, saying Coxon was correct. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” Hubinger wrote on X. “I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade.” The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. “Washington needs to wake up and take this seriously,” Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, said on X, referring to the risks of AI technology. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, on the TV programme “The View”, pointed to legislation to regulate AI’s “catastrophic risks”. Cruz oversees a Senate committee with oversight of the US Commerce Department, the agency with in-house AI safety researchers. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican from Florida, in a post on X called on House Speaker Mike Johnson to convene a “special session on AI”. The House is out this week on recess, with plans to return next week. But US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he did not have any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. “I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period,” he said in brief remarks to the media at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. The US this month pressed G20 members to take a hands-off approach to AI regulation. A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public at what some investors have said could be a potential $2 trillion valuation, said on Thursday that the company would continue to aggressively test “models or dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology”. The company is interested in working with the AI industry on the pace of releasing new AI tools, the spokesperson added. Other AI researchers have quit OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman told employees at a company meeting this week that the firm was open to slowing development of its AI systems, Bloomberg News reported . The Anthropic rival, which is also gearing up for an IPO, did not comment on Altman’s meeting with staff. The company has previously said it was slowing parts of model development. Earlier this week, OpenAI said it was pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements in the US. Two specialists in AI safety have also come forward with their concerns about the rapid development of the industry. Josh Engels, who used to work on AI safety research at Google DeepMind, said in an interview with NBC published on Thursday: “There are no adults in the room. People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.” Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, told NBC he is worried that AI might end up progressing “too fast for us to get our act together in time unless we worry about it now”. Both have joined METR, a research nonprofit that measures whether and when AI systems might threaten harm to society. Independent auditors Alarm about AI has put pressure on Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Democrat Amy Klobuchar, who are writing a bill to regulate AI products. Klobuchar said the legislation should require companies developing AI tools to “work with government experts to verify and test models to make sure AI is safe”. Thune told Reuters in July that the bill would address “catastrophic risks” posed by AI systems. California on Wednesday enacted the first state law setting rules for how independent auditors evaluate AI products. OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said OpenAI would support the bill, around the same time California Governor Gavin Newsom’s office released a statement saying he’d signed it into law. A bipartisan group of six US House lawmakers in July proposed legislation that ​would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits. The auditors would be accredited by ⁠the US Department of Commerce, and the department would create a new position to oversee AI security, according to the bill. “It is important to have space for oversight of these systems, including appropriately calibrated pre-deployment review and independent third-party audits,” said Alicia Solow-Niederman, a tech law professor at George Washington University.

Baber said the association remained in radio contact with Mehmood for about one-and-a-half hours after take-off, but his signal subsequently went offline. Local authorities fear that Mehmood may have crashed or been forced to make an emergency landing in the difficult terrain of the Barum hills. Rescue 1122 teams launched a search operation after his disappearance. The operation was suspended overnight due to darkness and poor visibility but resumed early on Friday. Local volunteers and administration officials are also assisting rescue teams as they search the mountainous terrain for the missing paraglider. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Friday suspended the operation of the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council’s (PMDC) directives ordering Afghan medical students to return to the neighbouring country. The decision came from Justice Khalid Ishaq, who was hearing a set of petitions filed by 13 Afghan students enrolled at different institutions in Lahore, including King Edward Medical University, Shaikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Medical and Dental College and the Services Institute of Medical Sciences. The pleas were filed after the PMDC issued a notification in September 1, directing Afghan medical students enrolled in Pakistani colleges “to return to Afghanistan”. The notification also barred medical and dental colleges from granting admission or placement to Afghan students for the current academic session. In their pleas, the students referred to the Sept 1 notification, as well as a July 31 directive, by the PMDC, and requested the LHC to declare them “illegal and unconstitutional”, without lawful authority and void from inception. Advocate Asad Jamal, who was representing the petitioners, further contended at the hearing today that the students had been condemned unheard and their rights to education, life and dignity had been violated as PMDC transgressed it’s jurisdiction under PMDC Act, 2022. He said the petitioners’ fundamental rights should be treated in accordance with law. On the other hand, PMDC’s lawyer Haris Azmat argued against the suspension of the council’s directives, saying that it was a matter of national security. Justice Ishaq, however, rejected the argument and ordered that the operation of Sept 1 and July 31 directives by the PMDC should be suspended. He further directed that students be allowed to continue education, sit their examinations and return to hostels. The judge also sought replies from the respondents, including the PMDC, health ministry and vice chancellors of relevant medical varsities and colleges, at the next hearing on September 18. Ferdinandh CABRERA / AFP Report 358 / Asia-Pacific 03 September 2026 20+ minutes Policing the Bangsamoro: Peace in the Southern Philippines Security continues to be a concern in the autonomous region of Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines. Law enforcement reforms and better coordination between the military and the police – as well as stronger gun control and better access to courts – could help stem the violence. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Philippines What’s new? Despite a 2014 peace agreement, crime and violence continue to rack the Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines. The military, which is still in charge of public safety, as well as the police and an array of local institutions are wrestling with outbreaks of fighting powered by easy access to firearms. Why does it matter? Local conflicts persist across the Bangsamoro, and the implementation of key provisions of the 2014 peace agreement remains well behind schedule. Entrenched clan feuds, political violence and criminal rackets make it hard to foster the trust in state institutions and social bonds needed to withstand future conflict. What should be done? Reforms to make regional law enforcement stronger, more professional and responsive to community needs are vital, as well as better coordination between the military and the police. Access to courts, control over firearms, and reinforced peacebuilding are also imperative to prevent the escalation of local violence and tackle its roots. Executive Summary The 2014 peace accord ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists in what is now the Bangsamoro autonomous region. But violence still flares as clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal rackets rattle the region. The police struggle to keep pace, leaving the military as the dominant security force. Other institutions remain ill prepared for the challenge. Courts are slow and often fail to guarantee justice, while institutions tasked with maintaining peace in the region have been afflicted by political infighting between factions of the former insurgent movement, and have yet to become fully operational. A clearer division of responsibility between Manila and regional authorities, along with a broader recognition of the roots of local conflict and the recurrent outbreaks of violence they cause, will be crucial to improving security conditions. At the heart of these efforts should be a reform of the police, bolstering recruitment, internal discipline and community policing. Tighter gun control, targeted justice reforms and peacebuilding initiatives should complement these efforts. After decades of war between the Philippine government and Moro rebels, progress toward curbing violence in the Bangsamoro region since it became autonomous in 2019 has been patchy. While the largest armed movement in the region, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), has renounced armed struggle and shifted its attention to the regional parliament and government, flare-ups of competitive political violence now outweigh rebel or militant fighting with the state. Clan feuds and electoral rivalries drive vendettas that regularly displace entire communities and weaken state authority. Criminal rackets are rife and firearms are easy to get hold of, fuelling cycles of violence. Key aspects of the 2014 peace agreement, including its security provisions, remain unfulfilled. This includes rebel disarmament, but also the redeployment of the military to other parts of the country and the disarmament of private militias. One of the biggest challenges in the normalisation process, as the region’s transition from war to peace is officially called, remains policing. The issue of who should be in charge of maintaining peace and order was the subject of intense debate during peace talks and in crafting the region’s autonomy law. Granting the regional government authority to handle public security was one option, but in the end Manila retained policing power in the region. Even so, the national police has struggled to define its role in areas of the newly autonomous region that remain affected by violence. Meanwhile, the integration of Moro ex‑rebels into the police force has been painstakingly slow. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. The military has earned public respect after decades of fighting a counterinsurgency in the area, but it is ill suited to handling local conflicts over the long run. Manila is grappling with how best to manage these dilemmas by continuing to deploy the military while using the police as backup. This approach, however, runs counter to the national government’s broader strategy of pivoting away from counterinsurgency to focus instead on external defence. For communities across the Bangsamoro hit by recurrent waves of violence, help is not always ready to hand. Communities often see the police as weaker, more politicised (especially due to local powerbrokers’ influence) and less dependable than the military. The regional government has greater powers over local dispute resolution and is in charge of building the local justice system, but is struggling to use its resources and is roiled by infighting. Long distances, case backlogs and steep costs mean local courts are often inaccessible to the Bangsamoro’s poorest citizens. The judiciary’s shortcomings are exacerbated by frequent score-settling between rival clans or bands, which can turn the filing of a legal case in court after a killing into the pretext for a fresh round of blood-letting and retaliation from the perpetrator’s clan. A rich tradition of community-based conflict resolution across the region offers alternatives, but its interaction with formal institutions has been uneven, and disputes often end up resurfacing. Both the national and regional governments should undertake reforms to mitigate violence and build a firmer foundation for handling threats to security. Supporting and professionalising the police is critical, but building a credible force will depend on practical improvements rather than sweeping reforms. Sustained efforts to rethink force structure, training and anti-corruption initiatives would help create a service responsive to the region’s needs. The police should also work to build better relations with communities, above all by addressing their most urgent concerns. Recruiting and training community safety police officers could be one way of bridging that gap. Ensuring better coordination between the military and police is also imperative. One solution would be for the military to gradually step back, enabling the police to take on more responsibilities for the management of public order. The relative calm in parts of the region should make this shift possible in at least some areas. These innovations should be accompanied by institutional reforms. The Bangsamoro needs sturdier mechanisms for settling disputes. Judicial reforms are also essential. For now, the formal justice system in the Bangsamoro remains weak, slow and too hard for its citizens to access, undermining public confidence in the courts. Strengthening Bangsamoro courts of all kinds with resources and personnel is paramount. Lastly, there are simply too many guns in the region for its citizens to be safe. Deterring gun use and clamping down on the supply of illegal weapons are essential to halt firearms proliferation. Together, these reforms should help curb the drivers of local violence, steer the region away from cycles of conflict and ensure law enforcement is in the hands of professional institutions that are responsive to the people of the Bangsamoro. Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs. Introduction For over five decades, a secessionist war raged in the Philippines’ southernmost island of Mindanao. The Muslim Moro people – who long experienced discrimination in the country – agitated for self-determination. 1 The term “Moro” refers to Islamised people in the southern Philippines, comprising thirteen ethno-linguistic groups. Two main armed movements representing Moro Muslim communities emerged: the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and its post 1977 splinter, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). 2 For earlier reporting on the peace process and transition, see Crisis Group Asia Reports N°355, Peace in the Philippines: The Bangsamoro’s Moment of Truth ; N°331, Southern Philippines: Making Peace Stick in the Bangsamoro , 1 May 2023; N°323, Islamist Militancy in the Southern Philippines , 18 March 2022; N°322, Southern Philippines: Fostering an Inclusive Bangsamoro , 18 February 2022; N°313, Southern Philippines: Keeping Normalisation on Track in the Bangsamoro , 15 April 2021; and N°306, Southern Philippines: Tackling Clan Politics in the Bangsamoro , 14 April 2020. The Philippine government deployed its military, paramilitary auxiliaries, and police against these groups. Over 120,000 people died in a conflict that did huge harm to public trust in state institutions and propagated the spread of weapons across numerous communities. The 2014 peace accord between Manila and the MILF – which provided political and fiscal autonomy to the Moro people within the boundaries of the Philippine state – marked a vital step toward reconciliation. In 2018, the Philippine Congress passed the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which voters then endorsed in a two-stage plebiscite in early 2019, thereby creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The Bangsamoro Transition Authority, an interim government led by the MILF, assumed power that February. The interim authority exercises self-governance in the Bangsamoro region, home to more than four million people spread across five provinces. The peace agreement foresaw two parallel tracks to achieve full Bangsamoro autonomy. First, former rebels would run the interim regional administration, pass new laws and build institutions. This political track was meant to conclude with regional elections in 2022, but these have been postponed several times, and are now planned for September 2026. Secondly, a “normalisation” agenda was to guide the broader transition from war to peace; it includes issues such as rebel disarmament but also socio-economic development and policing in the region. 3 The normalisation process does not have a set deadline and instead relies on qualitative milestones; both sides are meant to sign an “Exit Agreement” after they have met their respective commitments. As with the political track, however, the normalisation process has fallen behind schedule. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Kinship networks, entrenched political clans, diverse ethnolinguistic identities, and the uneasy coexistence of emerging political parties with armed movements all shape the region’s public life. Talking about his movement’s transition from guerrilla warfare to governance, a senior MILF commander admitted: “It was easier in the jungle”. 4 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Political tensions have also flared within the former insurgency. In March 2025, Manila replaced the region’s chief minister, MILF Chairman Murad Ebrahim, with the organisation’s military chief, Abdulraof Macacua. This change fractured the movement, pitting commanders and cadres loyal to the Central Committee against Macacua’s faction. 5 Murad is closely aligned with MILF’s chief negotiator and head of its implementing panel Mohagher Iqbal, who wields substantial influence over the movement’s political cadres. In response to Macacua’s perceived violations of internal regulations, the Central Committee suspended both him and eight loyal senior commanders from their roles, stopping short of expelling them from the organisation. The Bangsamoro region governs itself – the interim government, for example, exercises control over public finances – but the state’s use of force remains under Manila’s control. Specifically, the national government retains command over the police, while the armed forces play an active role in ensuring security. This arrangement reflects the national government’s enduring caution about a region with a long history of rebellion and the Philippine constitution, which mandates just one police force. 6 Crisis Group interviews, Manila, 8 May 2026. See also Article XVI, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Building on Crisis Group’s earlier work in the Bangsamoro, this report explores how public security is managed in the region, with particular attention to policing. It draws on years of field research in the Bangsamoro and Manila, including over 80 interviews with police and military officers, MILF commanders, representatives of the interim regional government, national and local officials, civil society figures, clan leaders, donors, villagers and decommissioned fighters. Women comprised around a third of interviewees. II. The Peace Deal and its Violent Aftermath Despite the undeniable progress made since the 2014 peace agreement, the Bangsamoro continues to grapple with security dilemmas. Although large-scale fighting has stopped, more than a third of young people across the region have experienced armed conflict within or near their homes since 2019. 7 Bangsamoro Youth Commission, “Bangsamoro Youth Assessment Study”, 2024, p. 60. A local civil society leader described the region as being in a state of “controlled peace”. 8 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Navigating sporadic outbursts of disorder remains particularly challenging for law enforcement. A. Conflict and Crime The national government now faces two main security threats in Mindanao. Its first concern are jihadist groups that have stayed out of the peace process and continue to fight the state. With the regional government’s support, Manila has managed to subdue cells from these outfits in the Sulu archipelago and contain groups in Central Mindanao. 9 Crisis Group interview, MILF commander, Cotabato City, 2 November 2023. The regional government has several programs to support fighters who gave up arms, and the MILF also played a role in influencing young Moros to cease armed struggle. But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025.
